result.text:
If Elon Musk ever loses control of SpaceX, SpaceX dies.

Not overnight. The rockets will keep flying for a few years on momentum. But the company that cut the cost of reaching orbit by more than 10x will become just another government agency.

Here's the proof.

First: a private monopoly is healthy.

Peter Thiel lays it out in Zero to One. Competition is for losers. A company in perfect competition fights to survive the next quarter. Its margins trend toward zero. It has neither the time nor the money to think 20 years ahead. A monopoly can afford to dream. Google funds moonshots. SpaceX funds Starship.

But there's a nuance almost everyone misses. SpaceX didn't get its position by decree. No law protects it. It earned it by being 10x better than everyone else, and any competitor is free to do better tomorrow. That's the difference between a monopoly of creation and a monopoly of the state. The first has to be earned every morning. The second is protected by force.

Second: the founder must stay king.

Founders Fund, Thiel's fund, was SpaceX's first institutional investor. Its doctrine is well known: never fire a founder, never vote against one. Back then, Silicon Valley did the opposite. You found a technical genius, then replaced him with a "professional manager" as soon as the company grew.

Thiel understood something simple. The value of a breakthrough company lives in its founder's head. The day you replace him with an administrator, you keep the chassis and throw away the engine.

That's exactly why SpaceX went public this year with super-voting shares. Elon owns about 42% of the equity but holds the overwhelming majority of the votes. The market signed anyway, eyes wide open, because the market knows where the value is.

Third: why Elon is irreplaceable.

Karpathy worked directly with him for five years at Tesla, and he has described his method. Small, deeply technical teams. No middle management. Low performers removed by default. Big useless meetings banned. He talks directly to engineers, and if the same bottleneck gets flagged to him twice, he blows it up on the spot.

In plain terms: Elon is one of the only humans alive who can run a giant like a startup.

Every organization that grows naturally secretes bureaucracy. Processes, committees, sign-offs, layers. That's entropy. Elon spends his life fighting it. He deletes, simplifies, cuts. The best part is no part.

Remove the man, and entropy wins. Mechanically.

Fourth: what happens when the state takes over.

A government official is never rewarded for success but is punished for every failure. So he minimizes risk. So he never does anything bold. It's not a question of intelligence. It's a question of incentives.

SpaceX built its entire method on failing fast. Launch it, watch it explode, learn, launch again. In a nationalized SpaceX, every Starship explosion becomes a congressional hearing. Every contract gets allocated by congressional district. Every decision goes to committee, and a committee seeks consensus. Consensus is the average. And the average doesn't go to Mars.

We already have the counterexample in front of us. The Space Shuttle, a public program, cost roughly $1.5 billion per flight over its lifetime. NASA's SLS costs over $4 billion per launch according to NASA's own Inspector General. A Falcon 9 costs around $70 million, and the booster lands itself.

Fifth: you need a madman with a vision.

In 2008, after three Falcon 1 failures in a row, Elon puts his last dollars into a fourth launch. If it fails, SpaceX is dead. It succeeds. A few months later, NASA signs.

Reusable boosters? The whole industry said it was impossible or uneconomical. No committee would have approved that bet. No bureaucrat would have put his career on the line for it. It took someone willing to be publicly wrong for years.

That can't be nationalized. You can seize the factories, the patents, the launch pads. You can't seize the will.

Conclusion.

Calls to nationalize SpaceX come from everywhere. From the radical left, but also from Steve Bannon in 2025. That tells you something. When a private company becomes more competent than the state, the political reflex isn't to learn from it. It's to capture it.

I believe we'll eventually move toward a separation of state and economy, the same way we separated church and state. For the same reason: when two powers mix, the more mediocre one contaminates the other. Politicians think in election cycles, entrepreneurs think in decades. Politicians seek consensus, entrepreneurs seek truth. Mixing the two is what rots everything.

The state should set the rules of the game. Not play it.

result.text:
While Piyush Goyal intended to play smart by bad-mouthing China’s business environment, he inadvertently exposed a deeply uncomfortable reality: in India, the ultra-rich are indeed very secure, precisely because they routinely stand above both the law and the people.

What many in India may not realize is that industries monopolized by large conglomerates in India—such as power generation, ports, and telecommunications—are state-managed in China. 

The reason is straightforward: these sectors are closely tied to people’s livelihoods and have natural monopoly characteristics, so they are judged by their capacity to serve society rather than by their profit-making ability. 

This is why China has long been able to keep electricity prices and freight rates low—they are backed by the power of the state.

By contrast, for most consumer goods, competition among Chinese companies is brutally fierce. The US has only Apple, but China has more than a dozen globally recognized smartphone brands; the US has only Tesla, but China has more than two dozen of EV brands.

Market champions are always the product of intense competition, because the government only sides with the final winners, and no Chinese company can sway government decisions the way Adani or Ambani do in India.

Having said all the above, it is not hard to see that Piyush Goyal’s remarks have unintentionally highlighted a major Chinese advantage: no matter how powerful capital becomes, it cannot override political authority. 

It is precisely this degree of political autonomy that allows Chinese decision-makers to remain free from capture by either commercial interests or populist pressures, and to make strategic choices that prioritize long-term outcomes and the interests of the greatest number of people.

1) I've sold a total of ZERO $TSLA shares and I am personally fully on board with Tesla's long term vision 

2) My primary point was that for the specific Tesla investors who ARE disillusioned, the reason is most certainly NOT a desire for more grandiose statements from Elon and Tesla. They simply want more actual results (profits) that are in line with these grandiose statements that have been made now for years

Example - on the Q1 call in '25 Elon said Robotaxi would be meaningful to Tesla's financials mid to late 2026 (paraphrasing). Here we are at that timeline and it's going to be another 12+ months. And guys, yes, I know he is just guessing here these aren't "promises". But if we can't at least acknowledge the public timelines given haven't been accurate than what are we doing here? The way I see it, this group of investors has valid arguments to be discontent

3) When I said "most Tesla investors," if it wasn't clear, I was referring specifically to the group that IS currently disillusioned and frustrated, not all Tesla investors in general. Although, I would argue that the number is certainly bigger than some would like to admit

4) What could Tesla do better? Not to sound like a broken record, but the biggest thing for me always comes back to setting expectations. Beyond that though - they could have continued making driveable vehicles a bit longer until autonomy was ready at scale. How about an EV under 30k with a wheel and pedals? A Cyber, proper 3 row SUV? A pickup truck that actually sells > 100k/year instead of ~20k?

There's just no way in my mind GM, Toyota and Ford should still be selling WAY more cars than Tesla annually in the US at this point

And again, I personally love the Cybertruck and love that Tesla takes these risks because I follow the company for FAR more than just the stock. But from the lens of investing, which this entire conversation is about, these decisions have been...questionable. Especially when you consider how many more folks would get to experience Tesla ownership and in turn FSD given all of the momentum right now, making the transition to autonomy even more seamless

I love Tesla, but no company is perfect. And I'm pretty sure Elon would agree that over the years, mistakes have been made. In the long run it will all work out - I haven't doubted that for one second, but I refuse to bury my head in the sand of sycophancy along the way $TSLA
